summary: Describes how to provide authentication and confidentiality to OSPFv3 by using the IPv6 Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload extension headers. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4552 explains how OSPFv3 routing packets use IPsec to check that messages are authentic and, when configured, keep their contents private. Its manual-key design cannot stop an attacker from replaying an old valid packet.

questions: how to secure ospfv3 with ipsec
does ospfv3 support ah and esp
why does ospfv3 use manual keys
subtitle: How OSPFv3 protects routing messages with IPsec authentication and encryption.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 removed the authentication fields present in the OSPFv2 header, so routing packets need protection from another mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: Routers use IPsec ESP for required authentication and may use AH. They use manually configured security associations, with matching parameters for inbound and outbound traffic.
tldr.outcome: The specification supports authentication and recommends confidentiality, but manual keys do not provide replay protection.

today: RFC 4552 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 Uses IPsec
sections.content:
OSPFv2 has authentication fields in its protocol header. OSPFv3 removed those fields and relies on IPv6 Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) for integrity, authentication, and confidentiality.

RFC 4552 specifies how OSPFv3 uses these IPsec headers. It assumes familiarity with OSPFv3, security associations, IPsec modes, and key management.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPFv3 does not carry the old authentication fields inside its own header. This specification uses IPsec headers to protect the routing messages instead.

sections.title: Authentication and Confidentiality
sections.content:
Implementations must support authentication and ESP. They may also support AH. ESP in transport mode authenticates the OSPFv3 packet, while AH also covers selected portions of the IPv6 header, extension headers, and options.

Confidentiality support is recommended and requires ESP. When authentication or confidentiality is enabled, packets that lack the required protection or fail its checks must be silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers must check protected OSPFv3 messages before accepting them. ESP is required for authentication support, and it is also required when an implementation provides confidentiality.

sections.title: IPsec Rules and Packet Selection
sections.content:
OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 both use IP protocol number 89, but OSPFv2 uses IPv4 and OSPFv3 uses IPv6. IPsec therefore distinguishes them using the IP version rather than an OSPF header field.

Implementations must support transport mode, multiple security policy databases selected by interface, selectors for addresses, protocol and direction, inbound interface tagging, and manually configured keys. They must also support IP encapsulation of ESP and must not let users choose stream ciphers for this manual-key design.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec selects the right protection rules using packet addresses, protocol, direction, and interface. The IP version separates OSPFv3 from OSPFv2 even though both use the same protocol number.

sections.title: Why Keys Are Configured Manually
sections.content:
OSPFv3 uses multicast as well as unicast. The RFC says IKE cannot provide the needed one-to-many protection for a broadcast interface, so implementations must support manual keying with statically installed security associations.

All routers on a link use the same security association parameters for inbound and outbound traffic. Administrators must be able to enter keys in hexadecimal so the available key entropy is not reduced by a restricted character set.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers on a shared link need protection that works for one sender and several receivers. The RFC therefore requires keys to be installed manually and consistently on the routers.

sections.title: Changing Keys Without Interrupting OSPF
sections.content:
The recommended rekeying procedure has three stages: add a new inbound security association on every router, switch every outbound association to the new key, then remove the old inbound association. Every router must finish one stage before any router starts the next.

The RFC recommends changing keys at least every 90 days. A configurable KeyRolloverInterval can give administrators time to update every router between stages.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can change keys in stages so packets remain protected during the change. The RFC recommends replacing the keys at least every 90 days.

sections.title: Replay Protection and Other Limits
sections.content:
Manual keying cannot negotiate sequence numbers for complete replay protection. An attacker may replay genuine OSPF packets, which can disrupt adjacencies, cause repeated database exchanges, consume CPU, or create routing micro-loops.

Long-lived or weak manually configured keys create further risks. Because routers on a link share key parameters, a compromised or misconfigured router may impersonate another router on that link.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid signature does not show when a routing message was sent. An attacker can replay an old message, and a compromised router that shares the key can impersonate others on its link.
